::: notes
The cards in place-value order, left to right: blue = 16, green = 8,
yellow = 4, orange = 2, red = 1 -- the order of the bits in a 5-bit number.
Point at each card's top-left number: it's the card's value, and every number
on the card has a 1 in that place.

Be sure to annotate -- the red card is the set of numbers with a 1 in the 1s place...

Red: a 1 in the 1s place (the odd numbers). Green: a 1 in the 8s place.
Telling me the colours tells me where the 1s are in your number's binary
representation, so adding the cards' values gives back the number (lecture 17).
Each card is a SET. Your number is characterized by which sets it belongs to.
:::

## The Word "Set" {.smaller}

A **set** is an unordered collection of distinct items.

* $\{1, 2, 3\} = \{3, 1, 2\} = \{1, 2, 2, 3\}$.

\

A set is often defined by a rule, $S = \{x : P(x)\}$.
$$\color{#3d9970}{\textbf{green}} = \{\, x : x \in \{1, \dots, 31\} \text{ and } x \text{ has a } 1 \text{ in the } 8\text{s place} \,\}$$

\

The items in a set are its **elements**: $x \in S$ exactly when $P(x)$ is true.

\ 

$24 \in \color{#3d9970}{\textbf{green}}$, because $24 = (11000)_2$. $\quad$ 
$18 \notin \color{#3d9970}{\textbf{green}}$, because $18 = (10010)_2$.

::: notes
For green, P(x) is "x is in 1..31 and x has a 1 in the 8s place".
24 = 16 + 8 = (11000)_2: a 1 in the 8s place, so 24 is on the green card.
5 = (101)_2: a 0 in the 8s place, so P(5) is false and 5 is not on it.
The rule is a predicate (lecture 8), and in pandas a predicate is a mask.
That's the bridge for the rest of the hour.
:::

## Meet the Class {.smaller}

Everyone gets an ID card. You are now one of the $100$ students in an imaginary DSCI 220.

\

* $U$ = all $100$ students: the **universe**.
* $\text{Room}$ = the students whose cards are here today. $\quad \text{Room} \subseteq U$.

\

Each card answers six yes/no questions. Each question defines a set: $\text{Coffee} = \{\, s \in U : s \text{ drinks coffee most days} \,\}$.

::: notes

from a shuffled stack: whoever comes gets one, and the cards left over are the
students who "didn't come today" -- still in U, not in Room. Put Amara, Ravi,

## Sets = Filters on Rows {.smaller}

\ 

Let $U$ be **all rows** of a dataframe `df`.

- A **set** $A\subseteq U$ selects rows by a **predicate** $P_A(x)$.
- In code, a set is a **Boolean mask**: `A_mask = P_A(row)`.

\ 

**Key Ideas**

- **Membership:** $x\in A \iff P_A(x)\iff$  mask on row $x$ is `True`
- **Cardinality:** $|A| = \sum_{x\in U} \mathbf{1}_A(x)\iff$ `A_mask.sum()`
- **Subset:** $A\subseteq B \iff \forall x, P_A(x)\Rightarrow P_B(x)\iff$ `((A & ~B).sum()==0)`

::: notes
Say: “We’ll reason with three parallel languages: math sets, logical predicates, and dataframe masks. They’re equivalent.”
:::

## Math ⇄ Predicate ⇄ Dataframe {.smaller}

$U$ is all the rows of `df`: the $100$ students in our class.

::: {.nowrap-code}
| Set | Set-builder | In pandas |
|---|---|---|
| $C$ | $\{\,x : \mathrm{coffee}(x)\,\}$ | `df[df['coffee']]` |
| $M$ | $\{\,x : \mathrm{morning}(x)\,\}$ | `df[df['morning']]` |
| $C \cap M$ | $\{\,x : \mathrm{coffee}(x) \text{ and } \mathrm{morning}(x)\,\}$ | `df[df['coffee'] & df['morning']]` |
: {tbl-colwidths="[9,37,54]"}
:::

<style>.reveal .nowrap-code code { white-space: nowrap; }</style>


::: notes
The set-builder drops "x in U": once the universe is clear we don't always
write it (contrast the green card, which spelled out x in {1, ..., 31}).
Same class as the cards. C and M are the sets from Hold Up Your Card, and the
third row is their intersection: the set C cap M, "and" in the set-builder,
& in pandas. The predicate sits inside the braces in math and inside the
brackets in pandas (df['coffee'] is the predicate as a True/False column); the
rows that come out are the set. In the class: |C| = 56, |M| = 45,
|C cap M| = 31.
:::

## Operations: Three Ways to Say the Same Thing {.smaller}

Let $A,B\subseteq U$.

| Operation | Math (set) | Predicate (logic) | Dataframe (mask) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Union** | $A\cup B$ | $\{x: P_A(x)\lor P_B(x)\}$ | `(A | B)` |
| **Intersection** | $A\cap B$ | $\{x: P_A(x)\land P_B(x)\}$ | `(A & B)` |
| **Difference** | $A-B$ | $\{x: P_A(x)\land \neg P_B(x)\}$ | `(A & ~B)` |
| **Complement** | $A^c$ | $\{x: \neg P_A(x)\}$ | `~A` |
| **Symm. diff.** | $A\triangle B$ | $\{x:(P_A\lor P_B)\land \neg(P_A\land P_B)\}$ | `A ^ B` |

**Precedence note:** use `&`, `|`, `~` with **parentheses**: `(A & B) | (~C)`.

## The Class in Code {.smaller .activity}

Fill in the "In all of $U$" column of the Hold Up Your Card table. 

```{pyodide}
#| echo: false
#| output: false
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/UBC-CS/dsci220/refs/heads/main/data/imaginary_class.csv")
```

```{pyodide}
C = df['coffee']
M = df['morning']

print("|C|     =", len(df[C]))
print("|M|     =", len(df[M]))
print("|C n M| =", len(df[C & M]))
print("|C u M| =", len(df[C | M]))
# your turn: |C - M| and the complement of C

print("|C| again:", C.sum())   # the same number: count the Trues
```

::: notes
Say once: len(df[C]) and C.sum() are the same number. len counts the rows of
the set; C.sum() counts the Trues in the mask (True is 1) -- the indicator sum
|A| = sum of 1_A(x) on Sets = Filters on Rows. Later slides use .sum(); it's
what students will see in real pandas code, and it never builds the subset.
A hidden cell above this one loads the class into df when the page opens (no
code or output shown); every later cell uses that df.
Answers for all 100: |C| = 56, |M| = 45, |C n M| = 31, |C u M| = 70,
|C - M| = 25 (len(df[C & ~M])), |C^c| = 44 (len(df[~C])).
Columns in df: name, tagline, coffee, morning, pet, games, cats, instrument
(all True/False), profile, card.
:::
